title: Write TOK Exhibition Commentary Beyond Description
summary: Learn how to write a TOK exhibition commentary that analyses knowledge, justifies each object, and stays focused during the IB TOK fall term.
body_markdown:
A strong TOK exhibition commentary does more than explain what an object is. It uses the object's **specific real-world context as evidence** , draws a clear conclusion about the selected IA prompt, and justifies why that particular object belongs in the exhibition.


The central shift is from **what happened** to **what this reveals about knowledge** . This guide explains the official requirements, a practical structure for each commentary, and methods for replacing description with focused TOK analysis.


### What the TOK exhibition officially requires


The exhibition is the internally assessed component of Theory of Knowledge. According to the[official IB TOK subject brief](https://www.ibo.org/globalassets/new-structure/programmes/dp/pdfs/tok-sb-english.pdf) , students select three objects and write accompanying commentaries exploring how TOK manifests in the world around them. It is worth **33% of the final TOK result** , is marked by the teacher, and is externally moderated by the IB.


You must:


- Select **one of the 35 prescribed IA prompts** and use its exact wording.
- Choose **three specific objects or images of objects** .
- Establish a **specific real-world context** for every object.
- Write commentaries totalling no more than **950 words** .
- Explain each object's link to the same prompt.
- Justify the contribution made by each object.
- Reference borrowed material and relevant factual claims appropriately.


Objects may be physical or digital, but each must exist in a particular context. Your annotated laboratory notebook or a named social media post could work. Broad categories such as “social media” or “a science textbook” are not sufficiently specific. RevisionDojo's[complete TOK exhibition guide](https://www.revisiondojo.com/blog/ib-tok-exhibition-your-complete-guide-to-success) provides a wider overview, but your school's internal deadline and submission instructions remain authoritative.


### Description, analysis, and justification


Description is necessary because the examiner must identify the object and understand its context. It becomes a weakness when it occupies most of the commentary without supporting a conclusion about knowledge.


Type of writing Purpose Example


Description Identifies the object This is a page from my chemistry laboratory notebook.


Context Explains how it functioned I recorded it during a titration that my group repeated after obtaining inconsistent results.


Analysis Develops a knowledge claim Repetition made the evidence more credible because the results could be checked.


Evaluation Qualifies the claim Agreement cannot reveal a systematic error shared by every trial.


Justification Explains the object's contribution The notebook shows how transparent procedures affect the quality of evidence.


Analysis stays connected to the object. Here, repeated titres and recorded corrections become evidence for claims about **reliability, method, and justification** .


### Build each commentary as a short argument


There is no compulsory paragraph template or official word allocation. With **950 words across three objects** , approximately 280-310 words per object is practical. Separate introductions and conclusions are optional and should be included only if they contribute meaningful analysis.


### Identify and contextualize the object


Name the exact object, including its creator, date, location, version, or personal connection where relevant. Instead of writing “This is a news article,” identify the named publication, publication date, and context in which you encountered it.


Include only contextual details that affect how knowledge was produced, communicated, disputed, or validated. Ask who created the object, why it was used, which audience encountered it, and which detail changes its knowledge value. The[RevisionDojo object-selection guide](https://www.revisiondojo.com/blog/selecting-the-right-objects-for-your-tok-exhibition) explains how to distinguish a particular object from a generic illustration.


### State an explicit prompt-linked claim


Do not expect the reader to infer the connection. Reuse important language from the selected prompt and state what the object suggests about it. Useful starting forms include:


- “This object suggests that, in this context, knowledge depends on...”
- “The object complicates the prompt because...”
- “What counts as evidence here is determined partly by...”


The claim must fit the actual object. It should not sound like a memorized sentence that could accompany almost any exhibition.


### Explain and qualify the knowledge mechanism


Explain **how** a claim becomes accepted, justified, interpreted, distributed, or challenged. Concepts such as **evidence, certainty, interpretation, perspective, authority, values, power,** and **responsibility** may help, but naming them is not analysis. If you mention bias, identify whose selection is biased, what was excluded, and how that affects the knowledge claim.


Then test the claim with a relevant limitation or condition. Repeated laboratory results may strengthen reliability, for example, while remaining inaccurate because of faulty calibration. This produces a precise conclusion: repetition supports reliability, but does not guarantee accuracy.


### Justify the distinct contribution


Explain why the particular object is useful and what it contributes that the other two do not. A coherent set might use one object to establish a case, another to introduce a limitation, and a third to change the perspective, method, or consequence. Three objects making the same argument create repetition rather than depth. RevisionDojo's[step-by-step exhibition guide](https://www.revisiondojo.com/blog/how-to-excel-in-your-ib-tok-exhibition-complete-step-by-step-guide) develops this planning approach.


### How to revise descriptive writing


Consider this description:


> This is my grandmother's handwritten recipe book. It contains old family recipes, and some measurements are not exact.


An analytical version might read:


> This recipe book contains instructions passed from my great-grandmother to my grandmother. Directions such as “add flour until the dough feels right” depend on practical familiarity rather than standardized measurement. This suggests that useful knowledge within my family includes embodied skills that cannot be communicated fully through precise language. However, that reliance on experience limits transferability because an outsider may not recognize the intended texture.


The revision retains contextual details that support a visible reasoning chain:


**Object detail → knowledge claim → explanation → limitation → prompt contribution**


Apply this chain to each paragraph. If a sentence does not support one of these functions, shorten or remove it.


### A practical September-November schedule


Your school's deadline controls your timetable. The following is advice, not an IB requirement, based on RevisionDojo's[Year 1 exhibition calendar](https://www.revisiondojo.com/ib/ib-theory-of-knowledge-tok/ib-theory-of-knowledge-tok-27-the-year-1-exhibition-calendar/notes) .


- **September:** Read the prompts carefully and collect more candidate objects than you need. Test each with one context sentence, one knowledge claim, and one distinct contribution.
- **October:** Select the final objects and draft all three commentaries. Check for overlapping arguments, verify contextual facts, and record source details.
- **November:** Revise for reasoning. Compare the amount of description with the amount of analysis, then check prompt wording, references, authenticity, and word count.


### Common mistakes to avoid


- Beginning with a broad history lesson rather than the object.
- Assuming personal significance automatically creates TOK relevance.
- Adding terminology such as “perspective” without explaining its effect.
- Mentioning the prompt once and leaving later connections implicit.
- Repeating the same knowledge claim across all three objects.
- Making unsupported claims about an object's origin or context.
- Turning the task into an abstract essay detached from the objects.


The[RevisionDojo TOK Exhibition Grader](https://www.revisiondojo.com/grader/rubric/tok-exhibition) can help identify weak context, justification, and prompt connections. Treat automated feedback as formative guidance and follow your teacher's instructions.


### Keep the work authentically yours


The[IB academic integrity policy](https://www.ibo.org/globalassets/new-structure/programmes/shared-resources/pdfs/academic-integrity-policy-en.pdf) explains that AI-produced material is not automatically the student's own work and must be acknowledged when used. A responsible use of Jojo AI is to ask which sentences are descriptive or which assumptions remain unsupported. Do not use it to produce submission-ready commentary, and ensure that you can explain every claim yourself.


### Conclusion


To move beyond description, provide only the context needed to make each object specific, then use that context to build an explicit argument about knowledge. Each object should support a prompt-linked claim, explain a knowledge mechanism, acknowledge a meaningful qualification, and make a distinct contribution. RevisionDojo's TOK Study Notes, Jojo AI, exhibition guides, and rubric-informed Grader can support revision while leaving the final reasoning authentically yours.
